questions.q: Name any two barrier methods of contraception and state the primary principle behind their action.
questions.a: Correct answer: Male condom and female condom (or diaphragm/cervical cap); they act by physically preventing sperm from entering the uterus and reaching the egg. A wrong answer like "copper-T and oral pills" reveals confusion between barrier methods and intrauterine/hormonal methods, indicating the student cannot categorize mechanisms.

questions.q: Explain why combined oral contraceptive pills (containing estrogen and progesterone) are taken daily for 21 days starting from the 5th day of the menstrual cycle.
questions.a: Correct answer: The hormones suppress FSH and LH secretion from the pituitary, preventing follicular development and ovulation; starting on day 5 ensures the pituitary is suppressed before the follicular phase begins. A wrong answer like "they kill sperm" or "they are taken only during intercourse" shows misunderstanding of hormonal mechanism and timing, confusing pills with barrier or emergency methods.

questions.q: A 28-year-old woman wants a long-term, reversible contraceptive that does not require daily action and has minimal hormonal side effects. Which method would you recommend and why?
questions.a: Correct answer: Copper-T (Cu-T) intrauterine device — it releases copper ions that are toxic to sperm, preventing fertilization, lasts 5–10 years, is reversible upon removal, and contains no hormones. A wrong answer like "oral pills" or "condom" fails to match the criteria (long-term, reversible, non-hormonal, low user-dependence), showing inability to apply method characteristics to user needs.

questions.q: Compare vasectomy and tubectomy in terms of procedure, reversibility, and physiological impact on hormone production.
questions.a: Correct answer: Vasectomy cuts/ties vas deferens in males; tubectomy cuts/ties fallopian tubes in females. Both are considered permanent but vasectomy reversal is more successful. Neither affects hormone production (testes/ovaries remain intact). A wrong answer claiming "vasectomy stops testosterone production" or "tubectomy causes menopause" reveals confusion between gamete transport and endocrine function.

questions.q: A student argues: "Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs) can be used as regular contraception because they also prevent pregnancy." Evaluate this statement.
questions.a: Correct answer: The statement is incorrect. ECPs contain high-dose progestin/anti-progestin to delay ovulation or prevent implantation after unprotected intercourse; they are less effective, have more side effects (nausea, menstrual irregularities), and do not protect against STIs. Regular use disrupts hormonal cycles. A wrong agreement shows inability to distinguish emergency vs. routine use based on mechanism, efficacy, and safety profile.

questions.q: Design a simple awareness poster for adolescents showing three contraceptive methods that also protect against STIs, with one key advantage and one limitation for each.
questions.a: Expected answer: Poster includes male condom (advantage: STI protection + easy access; limitation: user-dependent, may tear), female condom (advantage: female-controlled, STI protection; limitation: cost, insertion skill), and abstinence (advantage: 100% effective for pregnancy/STI; limitation: requires mutual commitment). A poor answer listing oral pills or Cu-T for STI protection reveals confusion between contraception and STI prevention.
